newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels in control of Zaire's Lubumbashi airport.
newsitem.headline: Rebels in control of Zaire's Lubumbashi airport.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels took control of the airport outside Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi on Thursday, capturing it from troops loyal to President Mobutu Sese Seko after a brief battle.

Witnesses said that the Mobutu loyalists, who had fled there after the fall of the southern mining capital on Wednesday, had gone into the surrounding bush. The airport was fully under rebel control by early evening.

"There was lots of fighting for about an hour-and-a-half in the late afternoon. It was terrifying, I can't put my fear into words," said Marie-Josephine, the wife of a local Zairean army soldier who surrendered and changed sides.
"Then the DSP (presidential guards) ran off into the bush. I would say there were about 250 of them in all at the airport... I don't think many people were killed."

Expatriate businessmen said earlier that up to 400 government troops had been trapped at Lubumbashi airport with heavy weapons they had threatened to turn on the freshly captured capital of Shaba province.
The rebels, who control half the sprawling Central African nation, moved into Lubumbashi on Wednesday after meeting stiff resistance on the approaches to the city.
The city was calm on Thursday afternoon apart from isolated gunshots. The rebels moved throughout the city, restoring order and ordering a halt to looting.

Doctors said they had received seven bodies of youths who they had been told were shot dead by rebels for looting after warnings not to. There was little sign of widescale looting except at military bases and at the homes of Mobutu aides.

Doctors and other medical workers said there had been very few casualties in the battle for Lubumbashi itself, but had no details of fierce fighting some 15 km (10 miles) away as the rebels approached on Monday.
Hospitals had only received a handful of civilian and military wounded. One missionary said three rebels killed in fighting had been buried in the morning.
Marie-Josephine huddled in an airport hangar with other women and children throughout the fight. She is from Kinshasa and would return there if there was a way.
Two planes sat on the tarmac, one flown in to take the Mobutu loyalists away but unable to leave for lack of fuel or a pilot.
Kabila's forces were drilling at one end of the runway. Others lay in the grass, exhausted. One said there had not been much of a fight before the Mobutu loyalists fled.
Trucks of rebels heading into Lubumbashi at dusk, the operation complete, were mobbed by enthusiastic townspeople.
The capture of the copper capital Lubumbashi, a few days after the diamond mining centre Mbuji-Mayi fell, leaves Kabila in control of the economic heartland which has financed Mobutu's 32-year rule.
More rebels streamed into the city on Thursday from the north as columns who had encircled it from three directions joined up.
People toppled or defaced statues and monuments to Mobutu's rule. Freshly daubed slogans read "Kabila is the new strong man of the Congo" and "Kabila is the right way".
Buildings flew white flags and the few vehicles in town tied white cloth -- a symbol of support for the rebels -- to their aerials.
